title: India's Biggest Medical Exam Has Been Cancelled Again. Two Million Students Are Running Out of Patience.
excerpt: The NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and a JEE Advanced data breach have reignited a national reckoning over exam integrity — and a new protest movement born from a cockroach meme is channelling the rage.
body:
For the second year running, India's largest medical entrance exam has been scrapped after a confirmed paper leak — and this time, the fallout has spilled onto the streets.

The National Testing Agency cancelled the NEET-UG 2026 examination, originally held on May 3, after evidence emerged that the question paper had been circulated before the test began. A rescheduled exam is now set for June 21. The Central Bureau of Investigation has opened an inquiry, multiple arrests have been made, and the NTA has warned students to ignore fraudulent claims on social media offering advance access to the new paper.

The cancellation follows a nearly identical crisis in 2024, when NEET results were voided after irregularities surfaced, including 67 candidates inexplicably sharing the top rank. That episode led to the Supreme Court intervening and the CBI taking over the investigation. For millions of aspiring doctors — roughly 2.4 million registered for the 2026 exam — the déjà vu is unbearable.

## A New Protest Movement Takes Shape

On June 6, hundreds of students gathered at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi under the banner of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP — a satirical protest movement that took its name from a remark by a judge who compared corrupt officials to cockroaches. What began as a social media meme has become a genuine vehicle for youth frustration.

The demonstrators, who had travelled from across the country, demanded the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the protest, underscoring its broadening appeal. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has also called for Pradhan's removal and an independent probe.

"We don't want less competition, we want fair competition," one student preparing for a national entrance exam told reporters. An UPSC aspirant from Noida put it more bluntly: "The education system is being destroyed. We have to raise our voice."

## JEE Advanced Breach Adds Fuel

The NEET scandal broke alongside a separate controversy involving JEE Advanced, the qualifying exam for India's 23 Indian Institutes of Technology. On June 5, IIT Roorkee acknowledged that a misconfigured cloud storage system had briefly exposed a small portion of exam data, though it insisted that less than 0.05 percent of read-only records were accessed and that no marks, ranks, or personal information were compromised.

The Education Ministry backed IIT Roorkee's account, calling the breach claims "misleading and factually incorrect." But the timing — days after the NEET cancellation — amplified public anxiety about the integrity of every high-stakes exam in the country.

## A Systemic Pattern

The back-to-back scandals have exposed what critics describe as a structural failure in India's examination infrastructure. The NTA, established in 2017 specifically to professionalise national-level testing, has presided over paper leaks in NEET (2024 and 2026), the cancellation of UGC-NET, and persistent questions about logistics and security.

In response to the latest crisis, the NTA announced a series of reforms: the appointment of senior oversight officers, a new chief technology officer to overhaul digital systems, and the introduction of AI-driven integrity controls and biometric authentication at test centres. Education Minister Pradhan chaired a review meeting pledging a "secure, seamless, and foolproof" re-examination.

Whether those assurances hold depends on June 21. For the students who have already spent years preparing, postponed their careers, and watched the same cycle repeat, the institutional credibility gap is now wider than the reforms are deep.

## The Diaspora Dimension

The exam crisis resonates beyond India's borders. Thousands of NRI families who send their children to study medicine in India — or who maintain the option as a backup — are watching the turmoil closely. The CBSE's separate controversy over its On-Screen Marking system for Class 12 board exams, which has produced reports of blurred answer sheet scans and technical glitches, compounds the concern.

A CNN profile of the CJP movement, published this week, framed the protests as a generational inflection point. A Boston University graduate who helped organise the campaign described it as a response to systemic neglect: India's demographic dividend depends on its young people trusting the institutions that credential them. That trust is now in open question.
